classification.difficultyReason: Must interpret the geometry before subtracting collinear triples, including checking whether lines through points on different sides create additional degeneracies.

content.prompt: A square with six distinct points chosen on each side is drawn.

spec.description: Unshaded square with six black points strictly inside each side and no marked corners.
spec.mathematics: Twenty-four distinct boundary points. Positions reproduce the visible regular arrangement; coordinates are drawing coordinates, not additional numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: All points and the square remain visible in the question edition; no triangles or solution marks are supplied.

children.prompt: How many triangles can be formed from the chosen points as vertices?

answer.short:
$1944$ triangles.

Choose any three of the 24 points and subtract triples lying on one side: $\binom{24}{3}-4\binom{6}{3}$.
answer.worked:
Three points form a triangle unless they all lie on the same side of the square. There are four sides, each containing six marked points.

$$\begin{align*}N&=\binom{24}{3}-4\binom{6}{3}\\N&=2024-4(20)\\N&=1944.\end{align*}$$

Alternatively, count triangles with vertices on three different sides, then those with two vertices on one side and the third on another:

$$\begin{align*}N&=\binom{4}{3}\binom{6}{1}^{3}+2\binom{4}{2}\binom{6}{2}\binom{6}{1}\\N&=864+1080\\N&=1944.\end{align*}$$

The factor of 2 chooses which of the two selected sides supplies two vertices.
